objective: The HIPAA breach notification rule as strengthened by HITECH: what counts as a breach, how risk is assessed and who must be notified
secondaryObjectives: The HIPAA Privacy Rule: who it covers (covered entities and business associates), what protected health information is, and which uses and disclosures it allows
Legal and regulatory frameworks as forces that shape health information behavior

sources.cite: HHS Office for Civil Rights, Breach Notification Rule (hhs.gov, HIPAA for Professionals)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. An impermissible use or disclosure 'is presumed to be a breach' unless a risk assessment shows a low probability of compromise from four factors: 'The nature and extent of the protected health information involved'; 'The unauthorized person who used the protected health information or to whom the disclosure was made'; 'Whether the protected health information was actually acquired or viewed'; 'The extent to which the risk to the protected health information has been mitigated'. Notification applies only to unsecured PHI; HHS guidance 'specifies encryption and destruction' as the methods that secure it. Individuals: 'without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 days following the discovery of a breach'. Media: a breach 'affecting more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction'. HHS: 500 or more individuals within 60 days; fewer than 500 within 60 days after the end of the calendar year. Covered entities have 'the burden of demonstrating that all required notifications have been provided' or that no breach occurred.

sources.cite: HHS Office for Civil Rights, Submitting Notice of a Breach to the Secretary
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: 500 or more individuals, 'No later than 60 calendar days from the discovery of the breach'; fewer than 500, 'Within 60 days after the end of the calendar year in which the breach was discovered'; 'a separate notice for each breach incident'.

sources.cite: AMIA Accreditation Committee, foundational domains for master's-level health informatics education (CAHIIM HI master's curriculum requirements PDF)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. F3 (Social and Behavioral Science) includes legal and regulatory frameworks; the MSHI course places the breach notification rule under F3 and cites 45 CFR Part 164 Subpart D.

Lakeview Health (fictional), its people, counts, costs and days are invented teaching values. The case works at the level of policy: no patient, record or message content appears. 'Without unreasonable delay' is a duty of its own; the case scores the 60-day outer limit and notes the duty in the debrief, and is not legal advice.

brief.situation: You are the health informatics lead on the privacy and security team at Lakeview Health (fictional). Monday morning, day 0, two reports arrive. A billing specialist emailed a spreadsheet of 1,240 patients (names, addresses, dates of service and diagnosis codes) to an outside address that autocompleted from a similar name; the recipient, at an unrelated company, replied that she opened it. And a care coordinator's laptop with about 2,100 patients' records cached was stolen from her car overnight. Of the 1,240 patients, 910 live in this state and 330 in the neighboring state.
handover: Lakeview is a covered entity. You work with the privacy officer and counsel; the privacy officer signs the breach decisions you prepare.
Your incident response budget is 60 thousand dollars. Letters with a toll-free line for 1,240 patients cost about 18 thousand; for 2,100 patients, about 30 thousand.
howItWorks: The clock runs in days: each task takes days. Choose it, then let it finish, which moves the calendar on.
The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words, the budget committed and the docket, including the notice deadline.
When you close the case you write the breach record and explain your reasoning.

compliant.headline: Good: presumed, assessed, notified, proven
compliant.body: The email was presumed a breach and the four factors did not rebut it, so 1,240 letters, media in the state with more than 500 residents, and HHS went out well inside 60 days. The laptop's encryption was shown before it was closed, which is the burden of proof the rule puts on you.

costly.headline: Within the rule, at a cost
costly.body: Every required notice went out on time. Something else slipped: the assessment came after the decision, the laptop's patients were notified without need, the COO was left unconvinced, or the cause is still open. 'Without unreasonable delay' is its own duty, too: 60 days is the outer limit, not the target.

outsideLaw.headline: A required notice was missed
outsideLaw.body: Deletion by the recipient does not end the presumption; per-state counts decide media notice but not HHS timing, which turns on 500 or more in all; and waiting for a review does not stop the 60-day clock from discovery.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No breach record was written before the case's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: An impermissible disclosure of PHI is presumed a breach unless a documented four-factor assessment shows a low probability of compromise. Diagnosis codes with names and addresses, sent to an unrelated outsider who read them, cannot show that, even with a deletion attestation. So notify each of the 1,240 patients without unreasonable delay and within 60 days; notify media in this state because 910 of its residents are affected (more than 500); and report to HHS within 60 days because 500 or more are affected in all. The laptop's data was encrypted with the key off the device, which makes it secured PHI and outside the rule, but the covered entity carries the burden of proof, so check the device record and file it. Then close the cause: outside autocomplete and an outbound rule for patient data.
